tierWindow.goal: Reflect on practice and work-based experience with rigour: understand experiential learning, use Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle to turn what you did into articulated learning, and meet how that learning is assessed.
tierWindow.cognitiveDemand: Analysis, application of a model, and articulation (explain, apply, analyse, articulate and judge), building on recognition and description assumed from earlier tiers.
tierWindow.taskComplexity: A model with interacting parts applied to the learner's own experience; the open, uncertain conditions of real practice rather than settled single ideas.
tierWindow.autonomy: Lower scaffolding than earlier tiers; one full worked reflection is unpacked, then the learner structures and judges reflection themselves; feedback explains reasoning rather than only confirming.

decidedValue.priorExperienceAnchor: The learner has already met practice- and work-based learning as a form of learning (the introductory tier) and has worked at making the most of an experience (the intermediate tier). This tier assumes they have done, or are doing, such an experience and are ready to reflect on it deliberately. It teaches reflection as the disciplined practice that turns experience into learning, not the idea that experience matters.

subThemes.label: Experiential learning: the idea that knowledge is created through the transformation of experience, not only through reading and listening
Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle: the four modes of experiencing, reflecting, thinking and acting
The two dimensions beneath the cycle: grasping experience (concrete experience and abstract thinking) and transforming it (reflection and active experimentation)
Using the cycle to structure a reflection on a real experience, as in the worked example of John's school placement
Why the cycle is a model to think with, not a fixed one-way sequence that must always run in the same order
How practice- and work-based learning is assessed, and why reflective practice sits at the centre of it
Articulating what you learned: producing a reflective account that evidences insight into your own performance and the workplace

decidedValue.courseOutcomeCountReason: Three, matching the three advanced sub-themes of reflecting on experience: understanding experiential learning and the cycle that models it (co1), using the cycle to structure your own reflection (co2), and articulating the resulting learning for how this kind of learning is assessed (co3). The introductory tier defines practice- and work-based learning and the intermediate tier makes the most of it; this terminal tier owns the deeper reflecting-on-experience material, so the outcomes move from understanding the model, to applying it, to articulating its product.

decidedValue.signpostBody: The course has three short lessons. First, learning through experience: what experiential learning is and the four modes of Kolb's cycle. Second, reflecting through the cycle: using those modes to structure a reflection, worked through a real example. Third, articulating what you learned: how this learning is assessed and how to evidence it. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
decidedValue.signpostInstruction: Work through the three lessons in order.
decidedValue.overview:
This course is about reflecting on experience: how to turn a practice or work-based experience into learning you can name and use. By the end you will be able to explain experiential learning and Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, use the cycle to structure a reflection, and articulate what you learned in a way that meets how this learning is assessed.

You have already met practice- and work-based learning and worked at making the most of it. This course takes the final step: reflection. Reflection is what turns an experience you had into a graduate who can say what they now know and will do differently.
decidedValue.courseOutcomesFraming: Three course outcomes framed up front: explain experiential learning and Kolb's cycle, use the cycle to structure a reflection, articulate what you learned for how it is assessed.

practiceConnection.academic: Reflection is the habit professional work runs on. Appraisals, placements, clinical supervision, teaching portfolios and chartership all ask you to look back at what you did, work out what it taught you, and act differently next time. Build a disciplined way of reflecting now and it carries into every placement of your degree and into professional practice beyond it.

decidedValue.summary: You have reached the end of the course. Reflecting on experience is no longer a vague instruction: it is something you can do with a method. You can explain experiential learning and Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, with its four modes and the two dimensions of grasping and transforming experience. You can use the cycle to structure a reflection, reaching every mode rather than following a rigid order. And you can articulate what you learned in a way that meets how this learning is assessed. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

practiceConnection.academic: From here, reflecting on experience is something you practise throughout your degree and beyond. Every placement review, every portfolio, every appraisal and every professional body that asks for reflective practice draws on the same method you have built here. The ability to take an experience, work out what it taught you, and act differently is what turns time spent into genuine development.
